title: Acute pairs and transversality
subtitle: G2 lecture 047000 · expanded mathematical companion
adaptation: Standalone companion adapted from the source spoken lecture and display-only mathematics appendix. Explicit hypotheses, stepwise proofs, worked examples, and local vector diagrams; no narration edits.

slides.title: Almost perpendicular versus uniformly separated
slides.lead: Every principal angle may be strictly below ninety degrees while some approach it arbitrarily closely.
body: For two closed subspaces U and V, distinguish the absence of an exact perpendicular intersection from a quantitative lower bound on cosine. In finite dimensions they coincide, but infinite-dimensional spaces can separate them.
That distinction controls whether a projection between subspaces has a bounded inverse and whether V is the graph of a bounded operator over U.
slides.takeaway: No right-angle vector does not imply a uniform bound away from a right angle.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 047000 · Almost perpendicular versus uniformly separated

slides.title: The two crossed intersections
slides.lead: The most direct obstruction comes from vectors that lie in one subspace and are perpendicular to the other.
body: If U∩V⊥ contains a nonzero vector, then projection from U to V destroys that direction completely. The analogous defect in the other direction is U⊥∩V.
Call the pair acute in the intersection sense when both crossed intersections vanish. This is a qualitative statement: it detects exact right-angle directions, not sequences of almost-right angles.
slides.takeaway: Acuteness excludes exact crossed-perpendicular directions on both sides.

slides.title: A stronger uniform gap
slides.lead: The operator-norm condition d=‖P−Q‖<1 bounds every principal angle at once.
body: The positive cosine C=(I−(P−Q)²)^{1/2} then satisfies C²≥(1−d²)I. Its spectrum stays uniformly above zero, so C has a bounded inverse.
On each principal plane d is the largest sine. The estimate gives the quantitative smallest cosine needed for stable graph coordinates.
slides.takeaway: Uniform separation gives bounded invertibility; qualitative acuteness alone does not.

slides.title: Why the cross-projection is invertible
slides.lead: The map P restricted to V sends a target vector to its U-coordinate.
body: For v∈V the uniform gap gives ‖(I−P)v‖≤d‖v‖. Orthogonality then yields ‖Pv‖≥√(1−d²)‖v‖: the coordinate map cannot collapse any nonzero vector.
The complementary gap condition on U rules out a missing target direction, making P|V a bounded bijection from V onto U. Its inverse has norm at most (1−d²)^{-1/2}.
slides.takeaway: A uniform lower bound gives stable coordinates between the two subspaces.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 047000 · Why the cross-projection is invertible

slides.title: Express V as a graph
slides.lead: Every v in V splits uniquely into an U-component and an U⊥-component.
body: When P|V is invertible, prescribe the first component u∈U and recover the unique v with Pv=u. Define Lu=(I−P)v; then V is exactly the graph of L over U.
The perpendicular component has norm at most d‖v‖ while the retained one has norm at least √(1−d²)‖v‖. Their ratio bounds the graph slope.
slides.takeaway: A uniform angle gap makes the target a bounded graph over the source.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 047000 · Express V as a graph

slides.title: One line: the tangent is the slope
slides.lead: For lines in the plane, the graph map sends the horizontal coordinate x to x tan θ vertically.
body: The norm of L is |tan θ|, while d=|sin θ|. Substituting into d/√(1−d²) recovers |tan θ| exactly for angles below ninety degrees.
This equality is the scalar geometry behind the operator graph bound. The denominator becomes small near a right angle, explaining why graph coordinates become poorly conditioned.
slides.takeaway: The tangent of the angle is exactly the graph slope in the planar model.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 047000 · One line: the tangent is the slope

slides.title: An infinite direct sum with no right angle
slides.lead: Take infinitely many orthogonal planes and rotate the source line in plane n by θₙ approaching π/2.
body: Choose cos θₙ=1/(n+2). Each angle is strictly acute, so there is no nonzero vector in either crossed intersection. But sin θₙ tends to one.
Thus ‖P−Q‖=1 and the graph slopes tan θₙ grow without bound. The two subspaces are acute in the intersection sense, yet V is not the graph of a bounded everywhere-defined map over U.
slides.takeaway: A sequence of near-right angles defeats uniform transversality without creating a defect vector.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 047000 · An infinite direct sum with no right angle

slides.title: Which hypothesis does a theorem need?
slides.lead: A theorem about existence of a polar direct rotation can often use qualitative acuteness.
body: If the construction uses a bounded inverse C^{-1} or bounded graph coordinates, it needs the stronger d<1 condition. The projection-based intertwiner K can have dense range but fail to be boundedly invertible when cosine values approach zero.
Check whether a proof genuinely divides by a uniform positive cosine. If it does, absence of a kernel by itself is not sufficient.
slides.takeaway: Inspect whether the argument requires injectivity or a uniform inverse bound.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 047000 · Which hypothesis does a theorem need?

slides.title: From graph geometry to rotation
slides.lead: Stable graph coordinates are especially convenient for comparing nearby invariant subspaces.
body: A bound on ‖L‖ yields a bound on the maximal principal angle through tan θ. A bounded graph also makes analytic perturbation estimates possible without choosing separate bases in U and V.
For larger angles the polar decomposition of the canonical intertwiner gives a more robust existence theory, whereas a graph parametrization may fail as the uniform gap approaches one.
slides.takeaway: Graph operators turn angle control into operator-norm slope control.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 047000 · From graph geometry to rotation

slides.title: Reconstruct the counterexample
slides.lead: The distinction between acute and uniformly acute is tested by an orthogonal sum of simple planar blocks.
body: Write the projections for two lines with cosine 1/(n+2) in each block. Show that the crossed defects vanish in every block and therefore in the whole Hilbert direct sum.
Then calculate sup sin θₙ=1 and sup tan θₙ=∞. The example proves that the strong graph condition cannot be inferred from qualitative acuteness.
slides.takeaway: Exact right angles and limiting right angles produce different operator phenomena.
